title: Expertly Introducing a Speaker
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that introducing an outside speaker is a more consequential leadership task than it looks, because the introduction sets the frame by which the talk will be judged. It claims that whatever the introducer highlights is carried into the audience's memory and linked to the speaker's content, and that the introducer's relationship to the speaker affects believability. The practical move is to replace a recitation of accolades with a few chosen facts tied to the audience or event, ideally drawn from what the speaker is proudest of. Humanizing touches such as why the speaker was chosen or what the introducer learned from them are recommended, while cuteness and embarrassing stories are ruled out. It closes by calling introductions stage-setting devices.
points: The introduction sets the frame for judging the remarks, so it carries more weight than most leaders assume.
Reading a blurb or listing accolades is called a weak move that fails to give the speaker useful context.
A better introduction selects a few impressive facts and ties them to the audience, using the speaker's own proudest items.
Making the speaker more human and approachable, for example by explaining why they were chosen, primes the audience positively.
Introducers should avoid getting cute or telling embarrassing stories, asking instead what will make the speaker more believable.
quotes: The introduction plays a bigger role than most leaders realize, as it sets the frame from which the remarks will be judged. Introductions create important context.

As introductions go, audiences don’t value or favor a long list of accolades, positions, and awards. Reading from a promotional blurb or profile is a weak move and doesn’t create the context most speakers need and desire.

The better call is to select a few impressive facts and to comment on them as they apply to the audience or the event. By asking the presenter for some items they are most proud of, the introducer can highlight those and draw a more personal connection to them.

Describing how the presenter came to be selected, what the introducer has learned from them, or why they are the perfect person to present at the event is a touch often used by good introducers. Anything that makes the presenter more human, more knowable, and approachable sets the stage in a positive way.

Good introducers don’t get cute, tell embarrassing stories about the presenter, or do anything that will detract from the presentation. Instead, they ask themselves what information they might share that will make the speaker more believable and their remarks more valuable.
Introductions matter. Treat them as stage-setting devices that allow presentations to sing. Everyone benefits when you do.
